title: 22. Interview: Distributed Tracing
summary: Interview Q&A for Distributed Tracing — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Distributed Tracing interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is distributed tracing, and why is it necessary in microservices but not in monoliths?
**Answer:** Distributed tracing records a single user request's path across multiple services as a tree of spans — each span representing one service's work, all sharing a trace ID — so operators can reconstruct the request's flow and pinpoint the slow or failing service. In a monolith, a slow request is debugged with per-function logging in one process — the call stack and logs show which function was slow, because everything happens in one process. In a microservices system, a single request fans out across many services, each in its own process, often on different machines; per-service logs cannot be correlated to a single request without a shared identifier, and the causal chain (A called B called C) is invisible. Distributed tracing solves this by tagging each request with a trace ID at the ingress, propagating it via headers through every hop, and recording a span per service. The assembled trace tree shows the entire request's flow with per-service latency, so the operator sees at a glance that inventory took 800 ms of the request's 1.2 s. Without tracing, the diagnosis is forensic log correlation across services — hours of work, often inconclusive. With tracing, the diagnosis is seconds. Uber and Twitter built Jaeger and Zipkin precisely because their microservices made per-service logs insufficient for debugging.
**Visual:**
```
monolith:    request -> func A -> func B -> func C   (one process, logs suffice)
microservices: request -> svc A -> svc B -> svc C   (separate processes, no shared view)
              per-service logs -> cannot correlate to a single request
tracing:     trace_id T1 + span per service -> trace tree in Jaeger
              -> see inventory took 800ms of 1.2s total -> diagnose in seconds
```

### Q2. Explain trace ID, span ID, and parent span ID, and how they form the trace tree.
**Answer:** A **trace ID** is a globally unique identifier for the end-to-end request (typically 128-bit hex), assigned at the ingress (the first service that sees the request, e.g., the API gateway). Every span in the request shares this trace ID, so the backend can group them into a single trace. A **span ID** is a unique identifier for one service's work on the request (typically 64-bit hex), generated by each service when it starts its span. A span represents a unit of work: one service's handling of one operation, with a start time, duration, service name, operation name, and tags (e.g., HTTP status, error). A **parent span ID** links a child span to its caller's span, forming the tree. When service A calls service B, A's tracer injects the trace ID, A's span ID (as parent), and a new span ID for B into the request headers (W3C `traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01` or B3's `X-B3-TraceId`, `X-B3-SpanId`, `X-B3-ParentSpanId`). B's tracer extracts these, starts a child span with parent=A's span ID, does its work, and propagates the trace ID to its own downstreams. The backend assembles spans by trace ID and links children to parents via the parent span ID, producing a tree with the ingress span as the root. The tree shows the request's causal flow and per-service latency at each node.
**Visual:**
```
trace ID T1 (assigned at ingress, shared by all spans in the request)
span S1 (gateway, parent=none, root)          dur=1200ms
  span S2 (order, parent=S1)                  dur=1100ms
    span S3 (inventory, parent=S2)            dur=800ms  <-- bottleneck
    span S4 (payment,  parent=S2)             dur=200ms
    span S5 (shipping, parent=S2)             dur=50ms
headers (W3C):  traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01
headers (B3):   X-B3-TraceId, X-B3-SpanId, X-B3-ParentSpanId
backend assembles by trace_id, links child->parent via parent_span_id -> tree
```

### Q3. What is OpenTelemetry, and why did it replace OpenTracing and OpenCensus?
**Answer:** OpenTelemetry is a CNCF project (formed in 2019 by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus) that provides a single, vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting, generating, collecting, and exporting telemetry data — traces, metrics, and logs. It has three parts: an API (used by application code to start spans, record metrics), a SDK (the implementation that batches and exports), and the Collector (a proxy that receives, processes, and exports to backends). Before OpenTelemetry, the tracing ecosystem was fragmented: OpenTracing (CNCF, vendor-neutral API, multiple backends) and OpenCensus (Google, API + library + exporter, narrower ecosystem) competed, and vendors (Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, AWS X-Ray) had their own libraries and APIs. A service instrumented with OpenTracing for Jaeger could not easily export to Datadog; a service instrumented with OpenCensus could not easily use Zipkin's UI. Switching backends meant re-instrumenting every service. OpenTelemetry solved this by providing one API and one SDK that export to any backend via configurable exporters — instrument once with OpenTelemetry, switch backends by changing the exporter config. The merger also brought metrics and (eventually) logs into the same standard, enabling correlation across signals (a trace span can link to the metrics and logs from the same request). OpenTelemetry is now the de facto standard for instrumentation; Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Datadog, and AWS X-Ray all accept OpenTelemetry data, and most vendors have deprecated their own instrumentation libraries in favor of OpenTelemetry.
**Visual:**
```
before OpenTelemetry (fragmented):
  OpenTracing (CNCF, API only)   <- Jaeger, Zipkin exporters
  OpenCensus (Google, API+lib)   <- Google Cloud, AWS exporters
  vendor libs (Datadog, New Relic, X-Ray) -> each with own API
  switching backend = re-instrument every service
OpenTelemetry (merged 2019):
  one API + one SDK + Collector -> export to ANY backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo,
                                    Datadog, X-Ray, etc.) via configurable exporter
  instrument once -> switch backend by changing exporter config
  also covers metrics + logs -> correlated telemetry across signals
status:  de facto standard; vendors deprecate own libs in favor of OTel
```

### Q4. What is the difference between head-based and tail-based sampling, and when do you use each?
**Answer:** Sampling selects a subset of requests to trace, because tracing every request is too expensive at scale (100k req/s × 200 bytes/span = 20 MB/s of trace data). **Head-based sampling** decides at request time, at the ingress, whether to trace — typically 1% of requests, random. The decision is propagated via headers (the `traceparent` `sampled` flag), so all services in the request know whether to emit spans. Head-based is cheap (one random decision per request), uniform, and simple, but it misses rare events: a 1% sample may not capture a 0.1% error rate, so errors go untraced. **Tail-based sampling** traces every request in memory and decides at the end of the request whether to keep the trace, based on the request's characteristics — keep all errors, all slow requests (latency > p99), and 1% of normal requests. Tail-based captures interesting requests at much lower volume (e.g., 5% of total volume, but 100% of errors and 100% of slow requests), which is what operators actually want to debug. The trade-off: tail-based requires holding the trace in memory until completion (the OpenTelemetry Collector does this), which is more expensive and adds latency to span emission. **When to use each**: head-based for high-volume, routine traffic where 1% sampling is sufficient and the simplicity is valued; tail-based for systems where errors and outliers must be captured (most production microservices). Modern systems use a combination: head-based 1% for routine tracing, tail-based for errors and slow requests via the Collector. OpenTelemetry's Collector supports tail-based sampling with configurable policies (e.g., "keep all traces with status_code=ERROR, keep 1% of others").
**Visual:**
```
head-based:  ingress decides at request time (1% random, propagated via header)
             cheap, simple, uniform -> MISSES rare errors (1% may not catch 0.1% errors)
tail-based:  trace all in memory, decide at END based on request characteristics
             keep all errors + all slow (>p99) + 1% of normal
             captures interesting requests at low volume -> MORE EXPENSIVE (memory)
when:
  head-based:  high-volume routine, simplicity valued, 1% sufficient
  tail-based:  errors + outliers must be captured (most production microservices)
combined:     head-based 1% routine + tail-based errors/slow via Collector
              (OpenTelemetry Collector supports tail-based policies)
```

### Q5. How does trace context propagation work across HTTP, gRPC, and message queues?
**Answer:** Trace context propagation is the mechanism by which the trace ID, span ID, and parent ID are passed from caller to callee across process boundaries. For **HTTP**, the W3C Trace Context standard (the modern default) uses the `traceparent` header: `00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-{flags}`, where `00` is the version, `flags` includes the sampled bit. The caller's tracer injects this header on the outgoing request; the callee's tracer extracts it and starts a child span. W3C also defines `tracestate` for vendor-specific extensions. The older B3 format (Zipkin) uses three headers: `X-B3-TraceId`, `X-B3-SpanId`, `X-B3-ParentSpanId`. Most systems support both for compatibility. For **gRPC**, the trace context is propagated via gRPC metadata (which is HTTP/2 headers under the hood), using the same `traceparent`/`tracestate` or `X-B3-*` headers. The OpenTelemetry gRPC instrumentation automatically injects and extracts. For **message queues** (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS), the trace context is propagated via message headers (Kafka record headers, RabbitMQ message properties, SQS message attributes). The producer's tracer injects the context when publishing; the consumer's tracer extracts it when consuming, starting a child span linked to the producer's span via the parent ID. The challenge with message queues is that the consumer may run long after the producer (async), but the trace tree still reflects the causal flow. OpenTelemetry supports all three transports with auto-instrumentation libraries, so application code does not need to manually inject/extract headers — the library does it transparently, as long as the application uses the instrumented HTTP/gRPC/message-queue client.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP (W3C Trace Context):
  header: traceparent: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-{flags}
  header: tracestate: vendor-specific extensions
  (older B3: X-B3-TraceId, X-B3-SpanId, X-B3-ParentSpanId)
gRPC:
  metadata (HTTP/2 headers under the hood) -> same traceparent/tracestate
  OpenTelemetry gRPC instrumentation auto-injects/extracts
message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS):
  message headers/properties/attributes -> traceparent/tracestate
  producer injects on publish, consumer extracts on consume
  child span linked to producer's span via parent_id (async, but causal)
auto-instrumentation: app uses OTel-instrumented client -> transparent, no manual code
```

### Q6. How does distributed tracing complement metrics and logs (the three pillars of observability)?
**Answer:** Metrics, logs, and traces are complementary signals, each answering different questions. **Metrics** answer "is something wrong?" — they are aggregated, numeric time-series (request count, error rate, latency percentiles) that show system health at a glance and alert on thresholds. Metrics are cheap to collect and store, but they are aggregates — they tell you the error rate is 5%, but not which requests failed or why. **Logs** answer "what happened in this service?" — they are discrete events with context (timestamp, severity, message, structured fields) that show what one service did. Logs are great for debugging one service's behavior, but correlating logs across services to a single request is hard without a trace ID. **Traces** answer "where in the request flow did it happen, and which services were involved?" — they show the end-to-end request as a tree of spans with per-service latency, so the operator sees that the inventory service took 800 ms of the 1.2 s request. The three compose: a metric alerts ("error rate spiked"); the operator opens a trace for a failing request ("inventory is slow"); they look at inventory's logs for that request's span ID ("the DB query took 750 ms"). The trace ID links metrics to traces (a metric can be tagged with trace ID for sampled requests), and the span ID links traces to logs (logs can include the span ID, so filtering by span ID shows all log lines for that span). OpenTelemetry's unified standard for all three signals enables this correlation natively — a single instrumentation library emits metrics, logs, and traces with shared context, so the operator can pivot between them seamlessly.
**Visual:**
```
metrics:  "is something wrong?"    aggregated, numeric, alerts (error rate 5%)
logs:     "what happened here?"    discrete events, one service (DB query took 750ms)
traces:   "where in the flow?"     end-to-end tree, per-service latency (inventory 800ms)
compose:
  metric alerts (error rate spiked)
    -> open trace for a failing request (inventory is slow)
      -> look at inventory logs for that span ID (DB query 750ms)
correlation:  trace ID links metric <-> trace; span ID links trace <-> log
OpenTelemetry:  one library, three signals, shared context -> pivot seamlessly
```

### Q7. What are the trade-offs and costs of distributed tracing, and how do you minimize them?
**Answer:** The costs are instrumentation effort, performance overhead, storage, and operational complexity. **Instrumentation effort**: every service must integrate the tracing library, and every downstream call must propagate the trace headers — missing propagation breaks the trace tree. Mitigation: use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation libraries (for HTTP, gRPC, DB drivers, message queues), which inject/extract automatically without application code changes; for custom spans, add a few lines per operation. **Performance overhead**: even with sampling, the tracing library adds CPU (header injection/extraction, span generation, batching) and memory (span buffers). Mitigation: sample aggressively (1% head-based for routine, tail-based for errors), batch span emission (avoid synchronous export), and use async exporters. **Storage cost**: trace data is voluminous even at 1% sampling — a service handling 100k req/s at 1% sampling generates 1000 spans/s, ~200 KB/s, ~17 GB/day. Mitigation: short retention (7–30 days), aggressive sampling, and compression (OpenTelemetry Collector can batch and compress before export). **Operational complexity**: the tracing backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo) is a distributed system to operate, with its own storage (Cassandra, Elasticsearch, S3) and scaling concerns. Mitigation: use managed tracing (AWS X-Ray, Datadog, Grafana Cloud) if operating a backend is too costly. **Adoption friction**: getting every team to instrument every service is a multi-quarter effort. Mitigation: mandate OpenTelemetry in service templates, provide auto-instrumentation, and make traces a required signal in the on-call workflow (so teams see the value and adopt). The deeper lesson: tracing is an investment that pays off in faster incident response and better system understanding; the costs are real but manageable with sampling, auto-instrumentation, and managed backends.
**Visual:**
```
costs:
  instrumentation effort -> use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation (no app code changes)
  performance overhead   -> sample aggressively (1% head + tail for errors),
                            batch + async export
  storage cost           -> 17 GB/day at 1% sampling; short retention (7-30d),
                            compression via Collector
  operational complexity -> use managed tracing (X-Ray, Datadog, Grafana Cloud)
                            if operating backend is too costly
  adoption friction      -> mandate OTel in service templates, auto-instrument,
                            make traces required in on-call workflow
lesson:  tracing is an investment; costs manageable with sampling + auto-inst + managed
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. A user reports that checkout is slow (5 seconds). Your system has 30 microservices. Without distributed tracing, how would you debug this, and how does tracing change the diagnosis?
**Answer:** Without distributed tracing, the diagnosis is a forensic nightmare. The on-call engineer would: pull the user's request from the API gateway logs (if a request ID was logged); search each downstream service's logs for that request ID (assuming each service logs it, which is uneven); correlate timestamps across 30 services' logs to reconstruct the call chain; guess at which service was slow based on which log lines have the largest time gaps. This takes hours, often fails (services without request IDs in logs are invisible), and produces uncertain conclusions ("we think it was inventory, but we can't be sure"). With distributed tracing, the diagnosis takes seconds. The engineer opens the tracing UI (Jaeger), finds the slow request (sorted by duration, or filtered by user ID if tags are set), and sees the trace tree: gateway 5 s -> order 4.8 s -> inventory 4.5 s. The trace shows inventory's span took 4.5 s, with tags showing the DB query took 4.3 s. The diagnosis is immediate and certain: inventory's DB query is the bottleneck. The engineer can then look at inventory's logs for that span ID, find the query, and fix it. The trace converted hours of uncertain forensic work into seconds of certain diagnosis — which is why Uber and Twitter built Jaeger and Zipkin. For any system above ~10 services, distributed tracing is as essential as metrics and logs.
**Visual:**
```
without tracing:
  pull request from gateway logs -> search 30 services' logs for request ID
  -> correlate timestamps -> guess at slow service (uncertain, hours)
  -> "we think it was inventory, but we can't be sure"
with tracing:
  open Jaeger -> find slow request (sorted by duration)
  -> trace tree: gateway 5s -> order 4.8s -> inventory 4.5s -> DB query 4.3s
  -> certain diagnosis in seconds: inventory DB query is the bottleneck
  -> look at inventory logs for that span ID -> fix the query
trace converts hours of uncertain forensic work into seconds of certain diagnosis
```

### Q2. Your team integrated OpenTelemetry in 5 of 20 services. Traces for requests that pass through the un-instrumented services show broken trees (the trace stops at the un-instrumented service). How do you fix this?
**Answer:** The broken trees are the classic "trace propagation gap" — when an un-instrumented service receives a request with trace headers but does not extract and propagate them, the trace tree breaks: the un-instrumented service's work is invisible, and any downstream calls it makes start a new trace (or no trace), losing the causal link. Three fixes, in order of preference. **(1) Instrument the un-instrumented services**: this is the only complete fix. Use OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation libraries for the service's language (Java agent, Python auto-instrumentation, Node, .NET, Go), which inject and extract trace context for HTTP, gRPC, DB drivers, and message queues without code changes — typically a one-line startup flag or a small dependency addition. For 15 services, this is a multi-week but high-value effort. Prioritize services on the critical path (those that handle user-facing requests). **(2) Use a service mesh with tracing**: if the services are enrolled in a mesh (Istio, Linkerd), the sidecar proxies propagate trace headers and emit spans even if the application does not — the mesh fills the gap for the network hop (though not for the application's internal work). This is a partial fix: the trace shows the sidecar-to-sidecar hops, but not the application's internal spans. **(3) Accept the gap and document it**: for low-priority services not on the critical path, accept that traces through them are broken, and document which services have the gap so operators interpret traces correctly. This is the weakest fix but may be pragmatic for legacy services. The long-term answer is full OpenTelemetry instrumentation across all services; the mesh is a bridge for services that cannot be instrumented quickly.
**Visual:**
```
problem:  un-instrumented service receives trace headers but does not extract/propagate
          -> trace tree breaks: service's work invisible, downstream starts new trace
fix 1 (best):  instrument all services with OTel auto-instrumentation
               (Java agent, Python auto-inst, etc.) -> no code changes
               prioritize critical-path services; multi-week for 15 services
fix 2 (partial): service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) sidecars propagate + emit spans
                 even if app does not -> fills network-hop gap (not internal spans)
fix 3 (weakest): accept gap for low-priority services, document for operators
long-term:  full OTel instrumentation across all services
            mesh is a bridge for services that cannot be instrumented quickly
```

### Q3. Your tracing backend is overwhelmed — span ingestion is lagging, and the UI is slow. The system handles 500k req/s, and you are sampling at 10%. How do you reduce the load without losing the ability to debug errors and slow requests?
**Answer:** 10% sampling at 500k req/s is 50k spans/s, which is too much for most self-hosted backends (Jaeger with Cassandra, Zipkin with Elasticsearch). Reduce load without losing debuggability via three changes. **(1) Switch to tail-based sampling at the OpenTelemetry Collector**: instead of head-based 10% (which traces 10% of everything, including normal requests), use tail-based sampling that traces 100% of errors, 100% of slow requests (latency > p99), and 1% of normal requests. This typically reduces volume to 1–3% of total while capturing 100% of the interesting requests (the ones operators debug). The Collector holds traces in memory until completion, then applies the policy. **(2) Reduce head-based sampling for routine traffic**: drop head-based from 10% to 1% (or even 0.1%) for routine traces, since tail-based captures the interesting ones. Combined with tail-based, this gives operators the errors and slow requests they need at much lower volume. **(3) Tune the Collector's batching and queueing**: increase batch size (e.g., 1024 spans per batch), increase queue length, add multiple Collector replicas behind a load balancer, and use a more scalable storage backend (S3/Tempo instead of Cassandra, or a managed backend like Grafana Cloud, Datadog, AWS X-Ray). **(4) Drop low-value spans**: configure the Collector to drop spans for noisy, low-value operations (e.g., health checks, metrics scraping) so only meaningful work is traced. **(5) Consider a managed backend**: if operating the backend is too costly, switch to a managed tracing service (AWS X-Ray, Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb) that scales ingestion for you. The combination of tail-based sampling (1–3% volume, 100% of interesting) and a scalable backend resolves the overload while preserving debuggability.
**Visual:**
```
problem:  500k req/s * 10% head-based = 50k spans/s -> backend overwhelmed
fix 1 (biggest):  tail-based sampling at OTel Collector
                  100% errors + 100% slow (>p99) + 1% normal
                  -> 1-3% volume, 100% of interesting requests captured
fix 2:  reduce head-based to 1% (or 0.1%) for routine -> tail-based covers interesting
fix 3:  tune Collector: batch=1024, queue, multiple replicas, scalable storage
        (Tempo/S3 instead of Cassandra, or managed: X-Ray, Datadog, Grafana Cloud)
fix 4:  drop low-value spans (health checks, metrics scraping)
fix 5:  consider managed backend if self-hosting is too costly
result: 1-3% volume, errors + slow captured, backend not overwhelmed
```

### Q4. Your service publishes messages to Kafka, which are consumed by another service 5 minutes later. How does distributed tracing handle this async, delayed flow?
**Answer:** Distributed tracing handles async flows via trace context propagation through the message headers, with the consumer linking its span to the producer's span via the parent ID — even if the consumer runs minutes or hours later. When the producer publishes a message, its tracer injects the trace context (trace ID, producer's span ID as parent) into the message headers (Kafka record headers, RabbitMQ message properties, SQS message attributes). When the consumer receives the message, its tracer extracts the context and starts a child span with the producer's span as parent. The trace tree shows the producer's span followed (possibly much later in wall-clock time) by the consumer's span, linked by the parent ID. The challenge with async flows is that the trace tree's wall-clock time may not reflect the causal latency — if the consumer runs 5 minutes after the producer, the trace's total duration appears to be 5 minutes, but the actual work might be milliseconds. To handle this, the producer typically records a "producer send" span (ending when the message is published) and the consumer records a "consumer receive" span (starting when the message is consumed), and the gap between them is the queue latency, which is visible in the trace. OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions for messaging define these spans (e.g., `messaging.publish`, `messaging.process`), so the trace shows the publish time, the queue time, and the process time separately. The deeper lesson: tracing handles async flows naturally as long as the message carries the trace context — the tree reflects causality, not just synchronicity, and the queue latency is visible as a gap between spans.
**Visual:**
```
producer (t=0):
  publish span (ends when message sent to Kafka)
  -> inject trace context into Kafka headers (trace_id, parent=producer_span_id)
queue (t=0 to t=5min):
  message sits in Kafka topic
consumer (t=5min):
  extract trace context from Kafka headers
  -> start consumer span (parent=producer_span_id, trace_id same)
  -> do work, end span
trace tree (assembled in backend):
  producer.publish span (t=0, dur=5ms)
    [gap: 5min queue latency]
  consumer.process span (t=5min, dur=20ms)
  -> total trace duration = 5min 5sec, but work = 25ms, queue = 5min
OTel semantic conventions: messaging.publish, messaging.process -> queue latency visible
lesson:  tracing handles async via message header propagation; causality, not sync
```

### Q5. Your tracing shows that a request to service A takes 2 seconds, but the trace tree shows A calling B (100 ms), C (100 ms), and D (100 ms), totaling 300 ms of downstream time. Where is the missing 1.7 seconds?
**Answer:** The missing 1.7 seconds is time spent in service A itself — not in downstream calls. The trace shows A's total span as 2 s, and A's children (B, C, D) as 300 ms total; the difference (1.7 s) is A's own work: CPU computation, DB queries, cache lookups, serialization, or just waiting between calls. To find what specifically, three steps. **(1) Add child spans within A for its internal operations**: instrument A's code with OpenTelemetry spans for its DB queries, cache lookups, computation, and serialization — e.g., `db.query users`, `cache.get preferences`, `compute recommendations`. These child spans (children of A's root span, siblings of B/C/D) will show where in A the time is spent. **(2) Check for "self-time" (un-instrumented code)**: if the child spans still don't account for the 1.7 s, the time is in code without spans — typically application logic between instrumented calls. Adding more spans (or using profiling tools that complement tracing, like async-profiler for Java or py-spy for Python) reveals this. **(3) Look for blocking operations**: a common cause of "missing" time is a blocking operation that isn't traced — a synchronous sleep, a lock contention, a GC pause, or a thread-pool wait. These show up as gaps in the trace tree, and they often indicate a bottleneck (e.g., A is waiting on a database connection from a saturated pool). The deeper lesson: the trace tree shows downstream calls explicitly, but A's own time is the difference between A's span duration and the sum of its children's durations — this "self-time" must be instrumented with internal spans to be diagnosed. Without internal spans, you know A is slow but not why; with them, you see that the DB query took 1.5 s and the cache lookup took 200 ms.
**Visual:**
```
A's span: 2.0s total
  B span: 100ms
  C span: 100ms
  D span: 100ms
  -> downstream = 300ms;  A's self-time = 1.7s (missing!)
diagnose:
  (1) add child spans for A's internal ops:
      db.query users: 1.5s      <-- bottleneck
      cache.get prefs: 200ms
      compute recs:     50ms
  (2) check un-instrumented code (profiling: async-profiler, py-spy)
  (3) look for blocking: sleep, lock contention, GC pause, thread-pool wait
lesson:  A's self-time = A.span - sum(children); instrument internal spans to diagnose
```

### Q6. You are building a new microservice and want to instrument it for distributed tracing from day one. What are the best practices?
**Answer:** Best practices for instrumenting a new microservice for tracing. **(1) Use OpenTelemetry**: it is the de facto standard, vendor-neutral, and exports to any backend. Do not use vendor-specific libraries (Datadog, Jaeger client) directly — they are being deprecated in favor of OpenTelemetry. **(2) Use auto-instrumentation first**: OpenTelemetry provides auto-instrumentation libraries for HTTP, gRPC, DB drivers, message queues in most languages (Java agent, Python auto-inst, Node, .NET, Go). These inject/extract trace context and emit spans for common operations without code changes — start here, and you get 80% of tracing value with near-zero effort. **(3) Add manual spans for business operations**: for operations not covered by auto-instrumentation (e.g., a custom computation step, a multi-step business workflow), add manual spans with `tracer.start_span("operation_name")`. Name spans after the operation, not the implementation (e.g., `process_payment`, not `handle_request`). **(4) Set span attributes (tags)**: add structured attributes to spans for filtering and searching — `user_id`, `order_id`, `tier`, `cache_hit`, `db.statement`. These make traces searchable ("show me all traces for user 123"). **(5) Propagate trace context in all downstream calls**: ensure every HTTP, gRPC, and message-queue call propagates the trace context (auto-instrumentation handles this; manual calls need `inject`/`extract`). Missing propagation breaks traces. **(6) Sample appropriately**: start with head-based 1% for routine; add tail-based at the Collector for errors and slow requests once volume grows. **(7) Test trace propagation in CI**: add a test that makes a request and verifies the trace appears in the backend with the expected spans — catching propagation regressions before production. **(8) Make tracing a required signal in the on-call workflow**: incidents must reference traces, so teams see the value and maintain instrumentation.
**Visual:**
```
(1) OpenTelemetry (vendor-neutral, exports to any backend; avoid vendor libs)
(2) auto-instrumentation first (HTTP, gRPC, DB, MQ; 80% value, near-zero effort)
(3) manual spans for business ops (process_payment, not handle_request)
(4) span attributes (user_id, order_id, tier, cache_hit, db.statement) for search
(5) propagate context in ALL downstream calls (auto-inst handles; manual needs inject/extract)
(6) sample: head-based 1% routine + tail-based errors/slow at Collector
(7) test trace propagation in CI (catch regressions before prod)
(8) make tracing required in on-call workflow (teams see value, maintain instrumentation)
```

### Q7. Your organization has metrics, logs, and traces, but the on-call engineers do not use traces during incidents — they rely on logs. How do you change this so traces become a primary debugging tool?
**Answer:** The pattern of having traces but not using them is common — usually because traces are siloed from the incident workflow, the UI is unfamiliar, or the traces are incomplete (broken trees from missing instrumentation). Three changes to make traces primary. **(1) Integrate traces into the incident workflow**: when an alert fires (from a metric), the alert should link to the tracing UI pre-filtered to the failing service and time window — e.g., "error rate spiked on checkout; click here to see traces of failing requests." This removes the friction of opening a separate UI and figuring out what to look for. Most modern observability platforms (Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb) support this; for self-hosted (Jaeger, Prometheus), wire the alert URL to include Jaeger query params. **(2) Make traces complete and trustworthy**: if traces have broken trees (missing instrumentation), engineers will not trust them. Audit instrumentation across all services, fill gaps with OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, and verify trace completeness in CI (a test that checks a request produces a complete trace tree). **(3) Train engineers to read traces**: a 1-hour training on "how to read a trace tree, find the slow span, pivot to logs via span ID" pays off enormously. Most engineers have not been trained on this, and the trace UI is unfamiliar. Pair this with a runbook that says "for slow-request incidents, open the trace first" — make the trace the default first step, not the last resort. **(4) Lead by example**: when senior engineers use traces in incident reviews and postmortems, the practice spreads. Reference specific traces in postmortems ("trace T1 showed inventory's DB query took 4.3 s") so the team sees the value. **(5) Make traces fast to access**: if the tracing UI is slow (overwhelmed backend), engineers will not use it. Invest in backend performance (sampling, scalable storage) so traces load in seconds. The combination of integration (low friction), completeness (trustworthy), training (capability), and example (culture) shifts the team to use traces as the primary debugging tool.

Head-based sampling decides at request time, at the ingress, whether to trace — typically 1% of requests, random. The decision is propagated via headers (the traceparent sampled flag), so all services in the request know whether to emit spans.
